t.1.37.1: Having related that tale to Rāma in sweet-syllabled words, Kauśika once again spoke these further words to Kākutstha.
t.1.37.2: Long ago there was a king, the valiant lord of Ayodhyā, named Sagara, righteous of soul; he longed for offspring, yet he was without children.
t.1.37.3: O Rāma, the daughter of the king of Vidarbha, Keśinī by name, was the eldest wife of Sagara; she was most devoted to dharma and always spoke the truth.
t.1.37.4: Sagara's second wife was the daughter of Ariṣṭanemi, named Sumati, unequalled in beauty upon the earth.
t.1.37.5: Then the king, together with those two wives, went to the Himavant and practised austerities on the mountain Bhṛguprasravaṇa.
t.1.37.6: Then, when a hundred years were complete, the sage Bhṛgu, foremost among the truthful, propitiated by austerity, granted a boon to Sagara.
t.1.37.7: O sinless one, you will have the great gain of offspring, and you will win incomparable fame in the world, O bull among men.
t.1.37.8: One of them, dear one, will give birth to a son who will carry on your line, and the other will bear sixty thousand sons.
t.1.37.9: Then the two royal wives, supremely delighted and with their palms joined in reverence, propitiated that tiger among men as he was speaking and said to him:
t.1.37.10: Which of us shall have a single son, O brahman, and which shall bring forth many? We two wish to hear it, O brahman; may your word prove true.
t.1.37.11: Having heard those words of the two women, the supremely righteous Bhṛgu spoke these excellent words: "Let your own free choice be exercised in this matter."
t.1.37.12: Let there be either a single son who will perpetuate the lineage, or many sons of great strength, renowned and of great energy; which of you desires which boon?
t.1.37.13: Having heard the words of the sage, O Raghunandana, O Rāma, Keśinī accepted, in the presence of the king, a son who would perpetuate the lineage.
t.1.37.14: Then Sumati, the sister of Suparṇa, obtained sixty thousand sons, sons of great energy and renown.
t.1.37.15: Having circumambulated the sage, keeping him on his right, and having bowed low to him with his head, the king went back to his own city together with his wife, O Raghunandana.
t.1.37.16: Then, when that time had passed, Keśinī, the elder queen, gave birth to a son of Sagara, who became known as Asamañja.
t.1.37.17: Sumati, O tiger among men, gave birth to a gourd-like embryo, and from the splitting of that gourd sixty thousand sons came forth.
t.1.37.18: The nurses reared them in pots filled with ghee, and after a long time they all attained youth.
t.1.37.19: Then, after a long time, sixty thousand sons, endowed with beauty and youth, were born to Sagara.
t.1.37.20: And that eldest one, O best of men, the son born of Sagara himself, O delight of the Raghus, would seize children and throw them into the waters of the Sarayū, and constantly laughing, he would watch them as they drowned.
t.1.37.21: Thus, given to wicked conduct, a hinderer of good people, and intent on harming the citizens, he was banished from the city by his father.
t.1.37.22: That Asamañja had a valiant son named Aṃśumān, esteemed by all the world and gentle of speech toward everyone.
t.1.37.23: Then, after a long time, O best of men, a firm resolve arose in Sagara: "Let me perform a sacrifice."
t.1.37.24: Having made his resolve, the king, versed in the Vedas, together with his band of preceptors, then set about the work of the sacrifice, beginning to offer worship.
